description: We’re Augustin, Simon and Joseph, a team of three taking part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We want to use NASA data to build an interactive project about space exploration. Our goal is to create a working prototype while learning how to work together and solve problems along the way.
summary:
We built Landfall to help people compare where and when to land on our Moon. Our web app combines interactive 3D views with precomputed Sun and Earth positions, so users can explore sunlight availability and direct Earth visibility at different sites and dates.

For Lunar Landing Site Navigator, we focused on what happens when plans change. Users set their own lighting and visibility requirements. When launch dates shift, Landfall checks whether their chosen site still meets those requirements and helps them explore alternatives.

These comparisons matter because sunlight affects solar power availability, while Earth visibility determines opportunities for direct communication. Guided exploration helps students and non-specialists understand these constraints, especially near our Moon’s south pole.

Landfall supports preliminary planning and education. Terrain results remain experimental, and meeting visibility requirements does not establish landing safety or mission feasibility.
details: Landfall lets users explore lunar landing sites through interactive 3D views and compare their lighting and Earth visibility over time. Users select existing sites or enter custom coordinates, choose dates, and examine conditions over 30-day periods. Site sheets show Sun and Earth positions relative to local horizons, visibility timelines, and countdowns to upcoming rises or sets. We focused on launch delays because changing dates can change whether sites meet mission requirements. Users define minimum sunlight and Earth visibility durations, along with their maximum acceptable night length. Landfall compares conditions before and after delays, then identifies alternative dates or sites within our dataset. Annual calendars make seasonal changes easier to explore. Our Python pipeline uses NASA/JPL SPICE kernels through SpiceyPy to calculate Sun and Earth positions. For selected southern sites, it also uses Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter elevation data to estimate terrain horizons. We prepare these scenarios in advance so users can explore results without repeating expensive calculations during interaction. Custom coordinates use geometric estimates that ignore terrain and carry explicit labels. Our development tools included: • TypeScript, HTML, and CSS for interface development. • Three.js and WebGL for interactive 3D scenes. • Vite and Node.js for development, asset preparation, and builds. • Python, SpiceyPy, NumPy, and SciPy for scientific processing. • Rasterio and PyProj for terrain data. • Blender to assemble and optimize supplied 3D assets. • Vitest, pytest, and browser testing for software checks. Our creative choice was to connect comparisons with visual exploration. Users can examine conditions and follow Starship through an illustrative descent to their selected site. Sun and Earth directions follow our dataset, while flight paths and nearby ground remain illustrative. Guided exploration introduces lunar planning through interactions with actual sites and dates. We want Landfall to make preliminary comparisons easier for mission teams and help educators explain why lunar landing decisions depend on timing. Different experience levels informed our interface: plain-language explanations appear alongside expandable scientific details. French and English interfaces, keyboard controls, and reduced-motion support help users explore at their own pace. Scientific limits shaped our design. Terrain results remain experimental. Earth visibility alone does not establish radio-link performance, and sunlight availability does not determine actual electrical output. Meeting user-selected requirements does not certify landing safety or mission feasibility.
